text: In the second year of his reign, Nebuchadnezzar had dreams that troubled his spirit so much that sleep left him.
So the king summoned the magicians, the enchanters, the sorcerers, and the Chaldeans to tell him his dreams; they came and stood before the king.
The king said to them, "I have had a dream, and my spirit is anxious to understand it."
The Chaldeans answered the king in Aramaic, "O king, live forever! Tell your servants the dream, and we will give its interpretation."
The king replied, "My decision is firm: if you cannot make the dream and its interpretation known to me, you will be torn limb from limb and your houses reduced to rubble."
"But if you can tell me the dream and interpret it, you will receive gifts, rewards, and great honor from me. So tell me the dream and its meaning."
They answered a second time, "Let the king tell his servants the dream, and we will interpret it."
The king said, "I see clearly that you are stalling, because you know my decision is firm —

if you do not make the dream known to me, only one sentence awaits you. You have agreed together to stall me with false and misleading words until the situation changes. Tell me the dream, and I will know you can interpret it."
The Chaldeans answered the king, "There is no one on earth who can do what the king asks; no king, however great, has ever demanded such a thing of any magician, enchanter, or Chaldean.
What the king asks is too hard, and no one can reveal it to the king except the gods, and they do not dwell among mortals."
At this the king grew angry and enraged, and gave orders to destroy all the wise men of Babylon.
So the decree went out that the wise men were to be killed, and men were sent to find Daniel and his companions to kill them too.
Then Daniel answered Arioch, the captain of the king's guard, who had gone out to execute the wise men of Babylon, with wisdom and tact.
He asked Arioch, "Why is the king's decree so harsh?" So Arioch explained the whole matter to Daniel.
Daniel then went and asked the king for time, so that he might tell him the interpretation.
Daniel returned to his house and explained the matter to his companions Hananiah, Mishael, and Azariah,
urging them to plead for mercy from the God of heaven concerning this mystery, so that he and his friends would not be killed with the rest of Babylon's wise men.
That night the mystery was revealed to Daniel in a vision, and Daniel blessed the God of heaven.
Daniel said, "Blessed be the name of God forever and ever, for wisdom and power belong to him.
He changes seasons and times; he removes kings and sets up kings; he gives wisdom to the wise and knowledge to those with understanding.
He reveals deep and hidden things; he knows what lies in darkness, and light dwells with him.
To you, God of my ancestors, I give thanks and praise, for you have given me wisdom and strength, and have made known to me what we asked of you — you have shown us the king's matter."
So Daniel went to Arioch, whom the king had appointed to destroy the wise men of Babylon, and said, "Do not kill the wise men of Babylon. Take me before the king, and I will interpret his dream."
Arioch quickly brought Daniel before the king and said, "I have found among the exiles from Judah a man who can make known to the king the interpretation."
The king asked Daniel, "Are you able to tell me the dream I saw and its interpretation?"
Daniel answered, "No wise man, enchanter, magician, or astrologer can explain to the king the mystery he has asked about,
but there is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries, and he has shown King Nebuchadnezzar what will happen in the latter days. This was your dream, the vision that came to you as you lay in bed:
As you lay there, O king, your thoughts turned to what would happen afterward, and the revealer of mysteries showed you what is to come.

As for me, this mystery has been revealed to me not because I am wiser than anyone else alive, but so that the interpretation may be made known to the king, and that you may understand the thoughts of your own heart.
"You, O king, were watching, and there stood before you a great statue — a single enormous image, dazzling and terrifying to look at.
The head of the statue was made of fine gold, its chest and arms of silver, its belly and thighs of bronze,
its legs of iron, and its feet partly of iron and partly of clay.
As you watched, a stone was cut out, though not by any human hand, and it struck the statue on its feet of iron and clay and shattered them.

Then the iron, the clay, the bronze, the silver, and the gold were all broken to pieces together and became like chaff blown from a summer threshing floor — the wind swept them away without a trace. But the stone that struck the statue grew into a great mountain that filled the whole earth.
"This was the dream; now we will tell the king its interpretation.
You, O king, king of kings, to whom the God of heaven has given the kingdom, the power, the strength, and the glory,
and into whose hand he has given mankind wherever they live, the animals of the field, and the birds of the sky, making you ruler over them all — you are that head of gold.
After you another kingdom will rise, weaker than yours, and after that a third kingdom, of bronze, which will rule the whole earth.
A fourth kingdom will be as strong as iron — for iron shatters and crushes everything — and like iron that smashes, this kingdom will crush and shatter all the others.
And as you saw the feet and toes made partly of potter's clay and partly of iron, this will be a divided kingdom, though it will retain some of iron's strength, as you saw the iron mixed with clay.
As the toes were part iron and part clay, so this kingdom will be part strong and part fragile.
And as you saw the iron mixed with soft clay, its peoples will mix with one another but will not hold together, just as iron does not blend with clay.

In the days of those kings, the God of heaven will set up a kingdom that will never be destroyed, one that will not be left to another people; it will crush all these kingdoms and bring them to an end, but it will stand forever —

just as you saw a stone cut from a mountain, though not by human hands, and it crushed the iron, the bronze, the clay, the silver, and the gold. The great God has shown the king what will happen after this; the dream is certain, and its interpretation trustworthy."
Then King Nebuchadnezzar fell on his face and paid homage to Daniel, and ordered that an offering and incense be presented to him.
The king said to Daniel, "Truly, your God is God over gods and Lord over kings, and a revealer of mysteries, since you were able to reveal this mystery."
Then the king elevated Daniel and gave him many great gifts, making him ruler over the whole province of Babylon and chief of all its wise men.
At Daniel's request, the king put Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego in charge of the affairs of the province of Babylon, while Daniel himself remained at the king's court.
